query: Historical timeline: how long do U.S. 123 nuclear cooperation agreement negotiations take from 'negotiations advanced/draft text' to formal signing? Recent examples 2015-2026
answer:
I've completed the research. The findings are in my report above, with the structured data submitted.

**The headline answer to your question:** the gap from a publicized "completion of negotiations"/initialing to formal signature has run **~2 to ~8 months**, median ~6.8 months across the three clean completed cases (South Korea 54 days, Vietnam 208 days, Saudi Arabia 246 days). Armenia is currently open at 191+ days.

**Three findings worth flagging as the most decision-relevant:**

1. **The completion-of-negotiations ceremony is itself a negative signal for near-term signature.** Most 123 agreements never have one — Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, UK, Mexico, and Norway all went straight from finished text to signature. The formal "Joint Statement/Declaration on the Completion of Negotiations" construction appears exactly twice, both Trump-era (Saudi Arabia, Armenia), and both are the slowest cases in the dataset. It looks like a device for giving a high-level visit a deliverable before the text is legally ready.

2. **The Presidential Determination is the real leading indicator** — it precedes signature by 4–7 days in five of six observed cases. That is the event to watch, not diplomatic statements.

3. **Renewals run close to the wire and sometimes fail.** China had two months of margin; Taiwan's entry into force landed exactly on the expiry date; South Korea missed its original expiry and needed a two-year act of Congress. Three agreements have lapsed outright. The South Africa case is the strongest caution for the Armenia situation: a stopgap extension was approved by Presidential Determination and transmitted to Congress in September 2022, yet was never executed because South Africa didn't complete its domestic procedures — and the agreement lapsed, costing Westinghouse its Koeberg export license.

**Two caveats on the data:** the Saudi congressional transmittal status is genuinely contested — Alhurra (Aug 4) and the Arms Control Association (Aug 7) both said it had not been sent, while a National Interest analysis (Aug 17) says it had. I could not resolve this and have reported it as unresolved rather than picking a side. Separately, mainstream media (Bloomberg, Al Jazeera, DW, NucNet, ANS) all reported Armenia's February joint statement as a signed 123 Agreement; only World Nuclear News, Reuters, and the Armenian PM's own office got it right. Any resolution source drawing on general news coverage may encode that error.

key_facts: The gap from publicized 'completion of negotiations'/initialing to formal signature: South Korea 54 days (Apr 22 2015 -> Jun 15 2015); Vietnam 208 days (initialed Oct 10 2013 -> signed May 6 2014); Saudi Arabia 246 days (Joint Declaration Nov 18 2025 -> signed Jul 22 2026); Armenia 191+ days and still open (Joint Statement Feb 9 2026 -> unsigned as of Aug 19 2026). Median of the three completed cases: 208 days (~6.8 months).

Most 123 agreements have NO separate public 'completion of negotiations' event — Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, UK, Mexico and Norway all went straight from finished text to signature. Both uses of the formal 'Joint Statement/Declaration on the Completion of Negotiations' construction (Saudi Arabia, Armenia) are Trump-era and are the two slowest cases observed, suggesting the ceremony is a political deliverable used when the text is not yet legally ready.

The Presidential Determination under AEA Sec. 123 b. (approving the agreement and authorizing execution) precedes signature by only days: UK 4 days, Mexico 7, Singapore 5, Thailand 4, Saudi Arabia 6. Vietnam's 71 days is the sole exception. A published Presidential Determination is therefore a near-immediate leading indicator of signature.

Signature to entry into force across all 25 bilateral agreements: median 232 days (7.6 months), mean 501 days, range 57 days (India) to 2,868 days (Turkey). Excluding the four outliers over 400 days, median is 199 days (6.5 months). For post-2010 signatures excluding Mexico and UK, median is 184 days (6.0 months), range 134-232 days.

Long signature-to-EIF tails are partner-side or geopolitical, never congressional: Mexico 1,640 days (Mexican Senate), UK 972 days (Brexit-dependent), Russia 980 days, Turkey 2,868 days. Congress has never disapproved a 123 agreement.

Renewals of expiring agreements are typically completed close to expiry, not well before: the U.S.-China successor entered into force Oct 29, 2015 with only ~2 months before the Dec 30, 2015 expiry; the Taiwan successor's entry into force (Jun 22, 2014) fell exactly on the predecessor's expiry date.

The U.S.-South Korea renewal missed the original expiry entirely. The 1974 agreement was to expire Mar 19, 2014; Congress enacted a two-year statutory extension (P.L. 113-81, Feb 12, 2014) to Mar 19, 2016. The successor was initialed Apr 2015, signed Jun 15, 2015 and entered into force Nov 25, 2015 — about 20 months after the original expiry date.

Three 123 agreements have lapsed without a successor: Colombia (expired Sep 17, 2013), Egypt (expired Dec 29, 2021), and South Africa (expired Dec 4, 2022). DOE revoked Egypt's and Colombia's Part 810 generally-authorized destination status effective Jan 31, 2023.

South Africa is the sharpest cautionary case: a 4-year stopgap extension was approved by Presidential Determination 2022-21 (Aug 25, 2022) and transmitted to Congress Sep 1-2, 2022, but the transmittal letter noted it 'will be executed once the Republic of South Africa completes its required domestic process.' South Africa never did; the agreement lapsed Dec 4, 2022 and the NRC suspended Westinghouse's Koeberg fuel export license on Jan 13, 2023. Negotiations deadlocked over South Africa's insistence on the right to manufacture its own fuel.

Agreements with automatic rolling extension terms renew without any renegotiation: Morocco (expired May 16, 2021), Turkey (Jun 2, 2023), and Euratom (Apr 12, 2026, now running to 2031) all auto-renewed. Japan's expired Jul 17, 2018 but 'remains in force until terminated by a Party.'

Upcoming agreements with NO specified renewal terms — requiring a wholly new negotiated agreement and congressional review — are Argentina (expires Oct 16, 2027), Ukraine (May 28, 2029), Brazil (Sep 15, 2029), Kazakhstan (Nov 5, 2029), and Indonesia (Dec 30, 2031).

Long gaps after lapse are normal where a partner is not urgent: Thailand's 1974 agreement expired June 2014 and its successor was signed Jan 14, 2025 (10.5 years later); the Philippines' predecessor expired in 1998 and its successor was signed Nov 16, 2023 (25 years later).

The Philippines negotiation (the fastest recent full cycle) was launched during VP Harris's Nov 2022 Manila visit and signed Nov 16, 2023 — 12 months elapsed, with the Philippine DOE stating negotiations 'took about seven months.' U.S. Ambassador Carlson said Oct 18, 2023 that talks were '90 percent done'; signature followed ~1 month later.

As of Aug 19, 2026 the U.S. has 26 123 agreements in force covering 50 countries, the IAEA, and Taiwan (per NNSA, last updated Jul 11, 2025). The three newest are Philippines (EIF Jul 2, 2024), Singapore (EIF Dec 12, 2024) and Thailand (EIF Jul 9, 2025).

Armenia's 123 Agreement remains unsigned as of Aug 19, 2026, 6.3 months after the Feb 9, 2026 completion of negotiations. Confirmed by expert Vahe Davtyan quoted in Caucasus Watch (Jul 29, 2026): the agreement 'has yet to be signed and must then be ratified in the United States and likely in Armenia as well.' Armenia's reactor technology decision has slipped to 2027 per Minister Khudatyan (Jun 11, 2026).

The Armenia joint statement explicitly frames the remaining delay as procedural: the two governments 'intend to proceed with their respective internal review and approval procedures, as well as any other legal steps, required prior to the signature and entry into force of the 123 Agreement.'

Saudi Arabia's 123 Agreement was signed Jul 22, 2026 by Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, alongside a bilateral safeguards agreement, following Presidential Determination 2026-18 of Jul 16, 2026 (91 FR 47715, published Jul 28, 2026). Negotiations with Saudi Arabia began in 2018 — roughly 8 years to signature.

Saudi congressional transmittal status is contested: Alhurra (Aug 4, 2026) and the Arms Control Association (Aug 7, 2026) both reported the agreement had NOT been sent to Congress, meaning the 90-day review clock had not started; a National Interest analysis (Aug 17, 2026) states the package 'was then submitted to Congress.' Unresolved as of Aug 19, 2026.

Media routinely conflate completion of negotiations with signature. Bloomberg, Al Jazeera, DW, NucNet and ANS all headlined Armenia's Feb 9, 2026 joint statement as 'signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement.' World Nuclear News, Reuters, Public Radio of Armenia and the Armenian PM's office correctly described it as a joint statement on completion of negotiations. Bloomberg's Nov 19, 2025 Saudi story is clearest: 'A formal 123 Atomic Energy Act agreement... has yet to be signed, a US Energy Department spokesman confirmed.'

Congressional review under the AEA totals 90 days of continuous session (a 30-day consultation period with SFRC/HFAC followed by 60 days before the full Congress). In practice the President transmits at the start of the full 90-day period. Non-exempt agreements enter into force automatically unless a joint resolution of disapproval becomes law; all Section 123 agreements in force are nonexempt.
